title: Limited money did not make the goal smaller
story: As a teenager, Fei-Fei Li moved from China to the United States with her family. She struggled with English while keeping up with school and helping her family financially through restaurant work and her parents' dry-cleaning business. She later received a scholarship to Princeton, studied physics, earned a PhD, and became a major figure in computer vision and human-centered AI. The useful part of her story is not that hardship automatically creates success. It is that she kept converting a large goal into the next available step while money and language remained real constraints.
turning_point: A scholarship did not appear because everything became easy; it became one more bridge in a path she was already building.

title: When the normal school route disappeared
story: Malala Yousafzai loved school, but when the Taliban took control of Pakistan's Swat Valley, girls were told they could no longer attend. At 11, she began writing about what was happening and later spoke publicly for girls' right to learn. At 15, she was attacked on her way home from school and survived. She continued her education and later studied at Oxford. Her story is not a demand that every student become an activist. It shows something more basic: disruption to school can be enormous without erasing a person's identity as a learner.
turning_point: She continued to treat learning as part of her future even when the ordinary route to school was violently interrupted.
match_reason: You selected school disengagement. This story is about separating 'school is difficult right now' from 'I am not capable of learning.'

title: A first step before there was a roadmap
story: Jan Koum moved from Ukraine to California with his mother when he was 16. His family lived with limited resources, and he worked while learning technical skills. He studied at San Jose State University, left college, worked at Yahoo, and later co-founded WhatsApp. His path into technology did not begin with a polished career plan or a famous startup network. It began with curiosity, self-directed learning and the next available opportunity. The point is not that everyone should copy his route; it is that a useful path can begin before the whole map is visible.
turning_point: The early breakthrough was not 'having the answer.' It was accumulating skills and experiences that made the next door visible.
match_reason: You selected lack of guidance. This story is relevant because it shows the difference between having no complete roadmap and having no next step.

title: Evidence can come before confidence
story: Ursula Burns grew up on New York's Lower East Side and chose engineering partly because she wanted an education that could change her family's economic future. She joined Xerox as a summer intern, then moved through engineering, product development and leadership roles before becoming CEO. Her career was not built by waiting to feel completely ready. It grew through repeated evidence: one hard task completed, then another role, then another responsibility. Confidence was not always the starting condition; it was often the result of action.
turning_point: Each completed responsibility became evidence that she could take on the next one.
